questions.q: What is the main cost/speed tradeoff between site-to-site VPN and a dedicated circuit like ExpressRoute or Direct Connect?
options: VPN is fast and cheap to set up; a dedicated circuit costs more and takes weeks due to physical provisioning
A dedicated circuit is always faster to set up than a VPN
VPN requires a physical cross-connect, while dedicated circuits are purely software-configured
There is no meaningful difference in cost or setup time between the two
questions.explain: VPN is a software/configuration task on both ends, often done in hours; a dedicated circuit needs a physical cross-connect at an exchange location, which takes real lead time.

questions.q: A workload has moderate, bursty traffic and no hard compliance requirement against the public internet. Which option is usually the right fit?
options: ExpressRoute or Direct Connect
Site-to-site VPN
Both must always be used together regardless of workload
Neither option can support this workload
questions.explain: VPN is well suited to moderate, bursty traffic without strict latency or compliance demands -- it's fast and cheap to stand up for that kind of need.

questions.q: Why would a compliance requirement push a workload toward a dedicated circuit even if traffic volume is modest?
options: Dedicated circuits are legally mandated for all workloads above a certain traffic volume
Some compliance rules require data never cross the public internet at all, which only a dedicated circuit satisfies, regardless of volume
VPN encryption is not strong enough to meet any compliance standard
Compliance rules always require the highest available bandwidth
questions.explain: A rule against transiting the public internet at all can't be satisfied by any amount of VPN encryption, since the traffic still technically crosses the internet underneath it.

questions.q: What is a common real-world pattern that uses both a dedicated circuit and a site-to-site VPN together?
options: The VPN as the primary path, with the dedicated circuit only used on weekends
Running both simultaneously for the exact same traffic with no failover logic
Using the VPN to encrypt traffic that already flows over the dedicated circuit
The dedicated circuit as the primary path, with VPN configured as automatic failover if it goes down
questions.explain: This pattern gets the dedicated circuit's consistent day-to-day performance plus a cheap, fast-to-restore VPN fallback if the circuit experiences an outage.

questions.q: Why isn't dedicated-circuit connectivity automatically the "better" choice over VPN in every scenario?
options: VPN and dedicated circuits provide identical performance in all cases
The right choice depends on traffic pattern, latency sensitivity, compliance needs, and how much setup time/cost the workload can tolerate
The choice is determined entirely by which cloud provider is being used
Dedicated circuits are strictly worse than VPN in every measurable way
questions.explain: Neither option is universally better -- the decision depends on the specific workload's bandwidth, latency, compliance, cost, and setup-time requirements.
